title: The Granth at home
hookLine: keeping a full Granth needs a dedicated, respectful room; many use a gutka or screen instead
tomorrow: should you read the Guru's words out loud, or in your head?

lines: A SPARE ROOM FULL OF BOXES.
FIRST, THE GURU NEEDS A HOME.
cards: Saturday morning, and a family stands in the doorway of a spare room. There's a treadmill nobody runs on, boxes of winter coats, a lamp missing its shade.
A relative has offered them a full saroop, a complete copy of the Guru Granth Sahib, for the reading they've planned. The dad is already measuring the wall. The grandmother crosses her arms.
Before the Guru comes home, she says, the Guru needs a home. And everyone turns to look at the treadmill.

teach.h: A FULL SAROOP NEEDS A HOME.
teach.b: She's describing a real promise. A full saroop isn't shelved like other books. Families who keep one give it a room or a corner of its own: clean, with a raised place, cloths to cover it, nothing piled around it.

teach.h: OPENED AT MORNING, RESTED AT NIGHT.
teach.b: In the morning it's opened, and at night it's closed and put to rest, the way a gurdwara does it. That's a daily commitment, not a decoration.

teach.h: A GUTKA OR A SCREEN, KEPT WITH CARE.
teach.b: So a household can keep the daily prayers in a gutka instead, or read the Granth on a screen, with the same clean hands and covered head. That isn't the lesser choice; it's an honest one. Now the turn.
In the Japji, Guru Nanak describes the world itself: nights, seasons, days, air, water, fire.

And in the middle of all that, in paraphrase, the earth is set down as a dharamsal, a place for living rightly. Something to tell someone tonight: in the Japji, the whole earth is called a place for dharma.
So a clean place isn't about square feet. It's about keeping. A shelf you keep clear is a better home than a room you forget.

how: Sikh families who keep a full saroop of the Guru Granth Sahib at home give it a clean room or corner of its own, opening it in the morning and resting it at night; others read the daily prayers from a gutka, or the Granth on a screen, with the same respect.

games.q: what does “the granth at home” mean?
o: a family's private gurdwara with its own granthi
keeping the Guru's words at home with daily care
a copy of the Granth kept mainly for display

games.q: a home for the Guru's words — tap the pairs.
p: a full copy of the Guru Granth Sahib
the daily prayers in a small book
the earth, a place for living rightly

s: a full Granth at home can sit on any bookshelf
families who keep a saroop give it a clean place of its own, and open and rest it each day.
reading from a gutka or a screen is the lesser choice
it's an honest one, made with the same clean hands and covered head.
in the Japji, Guru Nanak calls the earth a dharamsal
a place set down for living rightly, in the middle of nights, seasons, air, water and fire.

games.q: your cousin wants a full saroop at home, but the only free space is a desk in a busy hallway, piled with homework and keys. what fits today's teaching?
o: bring it home anyway; the respect is in your heart, not the room.
keep a gutka on a clear shelf until a clean place can be kept.
do nothing until the family can build a proper prayer room.
games.why: a full saroop needs a place kept clean and opened daily. a gutka, kept well, is an honest choice: a shelf you keep clear beats a room you forget.

practice: Look around wherever you are and choose one spot where the Guru's words could rest: a shelf, the corner of a desk, a windowsill. Just look at it while you breathe, and notice what would need to move.
You don't have to move anything yet; let the looking be the start of keeping it.

wordCard.voice: The Granth at home. A full copy kept with daily care in a place of its own, or a gutka or a screen kept with the same respect. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saroop, form; the word Sikhs use for a full copy of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: a clean place. Small is fine, as long as it's kept. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7 (Japji, Pauri 34: the earth set down as a dharamsal), paraphrased
Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the respect due to the Guru Granth Sahib (opening it in the morning, putting it to rest at night, a clean place), paraphrased
